title: Traumatic Brain Injury: Initial Assessment, Secondary Injury & Recovery
html:
Traumatic brain injury (TBI) ranges from concussion to contusion, diffuse injury, and life-threatening intracranial bleeding. The RN's job is to recognize high-risk head trauma, protect oxygenation and perfusion, detect neurologic change, support ordered imaging and treatment, and teach a safe recovery plan. A normal early conversation or initial CT does not replace reassessment when symptoms evolve.

Learning goals

  • Perform and trend a focused head-injury assessment rather than relying on a single Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score.
  • Identify red flags for urgent imaging, trauma or neurosurgical review, and possible intracranial bleeding.
  • Prevent secondary injury from hypoxemia, hypotension, poor ventilation, and delayed recognition of rising intracranial pressure (ICP).
  • Describe the nurse's role in ordered ICP, cerebral perfusion, seizure, and venous-thromboembolism plans.
  • Give appropriate concussion discharge education and return precautions.

First assessment: injury, airway, and neurologic baseline

Use a trauma primary survey and maintain cervical-spine precautions when indicated. Note the mechanism and time of injury, loss of consciousness or amnesia, vomiting, seizure, headache, anticoagulant or antiplatelet use, intoxication, and baseline cognition. Reassess airway protection and breathing; depressed consciousness and vomiting increase aspiration risk. Document GCS eye, verbal, and motor components as well as the total, then compare serially. Examine pupils, limb movement and symmetry, speech, behavior, orientation, and vital signs. Record factors that make the examination less reliable, such as sedation, paralytics, intoxication, or preexisting deficits. A falling motor response, new focal deficit, unequal pupils, seizure, or increasing confusion is an urgent change even if an earlier score looked reassuring.

Imaging and deterioration

Noncontrast head CT is a key early test when clinical risk factors are present; the treating clinician applies current adult head-injury criteria and local pathways. Urgent review is especially important after worsening consciousness, focal findings, post-traumatic seizure, repeated vomiting, signs of skull fracture, or a concerning mechanism. Anticoagulant treatment or most antiplatelet regimens can lower the threshold for CT consideration even without other signs; aspirin alone is treated differently in NICE's specific recommendation. Verify the exact drug and last dose, and report bleeding risks. Do not independently stop or reverse medication for every head injury; reversal is a specialist-directed decision when traumatic intracranial hemorrhage or another indication is identified. If the examination worsens after a reassuring scan, escalate for repeat evaluation rather than assuming the first image remains definitive.

Extra-axial bleeding such as epidural or subdural hematoma may cause mass effect; contusions can also evolve. A so-called lucid interval is possible but is not required for any diagnosis. Repeated neurologic observations, not a textbook pattern, reveal change. Keep the patient under the level of observation ordered for their risk, report a sustained or new decline immediately, and prepare for neurosurgical assessment or transfer when indicated.

Prevent secondary brain injury

The initial mechanical trauma is already present; subsequent hypoxemia, hypotension, impaired ventilation, fever, seizure, or expanding hemorrhage can worsen injury. Monitor airway patency, oxygenation, respiratory pattern, blood pressure, temperature, glucose, and urine output in the context of the care plan. Follow ordered resuscitation and avoid preventable hypotension; rapidly identify other traumatic bleeding. For severe TBI, ICP and cerebral perfusion pressure (CPP = mean arterial pressure − ICP) may be monitored to guide specialist treatment. Brain Trauma Foundation guidance recommends treating sustained ICP above 22 mm Hg and suggests a CPP target of 60–70 mm Hg, but bedside decisions use the full clinical picture and individualized orders, not a single number. Position the head and neck to promote venous drainage when safe, avoid unnecessary stimulation and neck compression, and coordinate with spine precautions. Hyperosmolar therapy, cerebrospinal fluid drainage, sedation, surgery, and seizure prophylaxis require orders and protocol-specific monitoring. Routine prolonged prophylactic hyperventilation is not recommended; it can reduce cerebral blood flow. Steroids are not a treatment for severe TBI-related swelling and may cause harm.

ICU nursing surveillance and complication prevention

Compare neurologic findings and ICP or CPP trends with the patient's own baseline, and correlate them with oxygenation, blood pressure, sedation, fever, and imaging. If an external ventricular drain is present, follow the unit's leveling, drainage, clamping, and infection-prevention protocol; do not change settings independently. Monitor ordered therapy for hypotension, sodium and fluid disturbances, renal concerns, or oversedation. Follow a swallow and aspiration plan before oral intake. Prevent pressure injury and delirium, provide nutrition and early rehabilitation as appropriate, and use mechanical or ordered pharmacologic venous-thromboembolism prevention only when the bleeding risk and brain imaging permit it. Keep family informed in clear language and avoid predicting recovery from an early single examination.

Mild TBI and concussion: safe discharge

Concussion can cause headache, dizziness, light or noise sensitivity, sleep disruption, slowed thinking, and emotional symptoms without a visible CT lesion. Before discharge, verify that the clinician's imaging or observation decision, home supervision, written instructions, and follow-up are clear. Teach the patient and a responsible adult to seek urgent care for worsening headache, repeated vomiting, increasing confusion, new weakness, seizure, or trouble waking. CDC guidance supports brief initial rest followed by a gradual, symptom-guided return to light activity; prolonged strict bed rest is not the default. Avoid another head injury, ask before returning to driving or risky work, and arrange follow-up if symptoms persist or worsen.

Apply clinical judgment

  1. Recognize cues: Collect injury mechanism, neurologic baseline and trend, medication exposure, vomiting or seizure, airway status, and vital signs.
  2. Analyze cues: Separate primary injury from preventable secondary insults and consider evolving hemorrhage when consciousness or focal findings change.
  3. Prioritize hypotheses: Threatened airway, hypoxemia, hypotension, expanding bleed, and acute neurologic decline outrank routine teaching or mobility.
  4. Generate solutions: Prepare airway and perfusion support, prescribed monitoring, head CT and neurosurgical review, safe medication decisions, and family communication.
  5. Take action: Escalate new findings immediately, perform serial documented examinations, give ordered treatment, and use spine and aspiration precautions as indicated.
  6. Evaluate outcomes: Confirm stable or improving neurologic examination, oxygenation, perfusion, treatment tolerance, safe disposition, and understanding of return precautions.

Clinical example

An older adult taking apixaban falls and initially answers questions normally. Two hours later, speech is slower, the motor response is weaker on the left, and a new headache appears. The RN repeats and documents the focused neurologic examination, calls the emergency or trauma team, verifies the anticoagulant and last dose, prepares for urgent imaging and possible specialist-directed reversal, and protects airway and perfusion. The patient is not reassured solely by the initially normal conversation.
